prompt: Match each loss to the summary of the target it aims at.
hint: Absolute error and squared error aim at different middles.

prompt: `errors.py` ranks `boost_absolute` first by MAE and the line first by RMSE. What does that tell you?
hint: Each metric measures a different kind of mistake.

choices.text: The line overfits
choices.why: Nothing in the table shows overfitting.

choices.text: One of the two metrics has a bug in scikit-learn
choices.why: Both are correct; they measure different things.

choices.text: The test months are too short for either metric to be trusted
choices.why: 1,540 deliveries is plenty; the disagreement is about what is measured.

choices.text: They reward different mistakes
choices.why: Yes. MAE weighs every minute alike; RMSE weighs the big misses most.

prompt: Five deliveries took 30, 32, 35, 40 and 120 minutes. What total absolute error does a guess of 40 give?
Why is MAE the easiest of the four metrics to explain to a logistics manager?

choices.text: It is in minutes
choices.why: Yes. "Off by five minutes" needs no translation.

choices.text: It ignores the deliveries that went wrong
choices.why: It counts every delivery in proportion to its error.

choices.text: It is always the smallest of the four numbers
choices.why: Being small is not being clear, and MAPE and R² are on other scales.

choices.text: It is the default metric that `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` uses when fitting
choices.why: The default loss is squared error.

prompt: The MAE is smallest when every prediction is the ___ of the truth for that kind of case.
In squared error, how many errors of 10 minutes weigh as much as one error of 60 minutes?
Without the deliveries more than 30 minutes off, the line's RMSE falls from 14.25 to 4.58. What does that show?

choices.text: The stuck deliveries should be deleted from the data before fitting any model
choices.why: They happen; deleting them hides real delays from the promise.

choices.text: Those 46 deliveries make up most of the RMSE
choices.why: Yes. Squaring hands the metric to the few big misses.

choices.text: RMSE was computed wrongly
choices.why: It is the same formula on fewer rows.

choices.text: The line is a poor model
choices.why: Its MAE without them is 3.76 minutes.

prompt: RMSE is 14.43 and MAE is 5.02 for the same model. What does the gap say?
hint: When would the two be equal?

choices.text: The model is biased towards being late
choices.why: Neither metric keeps the sign of the error.

choices.text: RMSE uses the training months and MAE the test months
choices.why: Both use the same test predictions.

choices.text: The errors have a heavy tail
choices.why: Yes. With errors of similar size the two would be close.

choices.text: The model is three times worse than it looks
choices.why: Both are true descriptions of the same errors.

prompt: A delivery of 20 minutes was predicted at 25. What is its absolute percentage error, in percent?
Why does choosing a model by MAPE pull it towards predicting too little?
hint: What is the most an under-prediction can cost?

choices.text: Percentages are smaller for long deliveries
choices.why: True, but that does not set a direction.

choices.text: MAPE is fitted by squared error
choices.why: MAPE is a metric, not a loss anybody fitted here.

choices.text: MAPE ignores errors below the truth
choices.why: It counts them; it just caps them at 100%.

choices.text: Predicting low costs at most 100%; predicting high has no ceiling
choices.why: Yes. The division makes the two sides unequal.

prompt: On which target is MAPE meaningless?

choices.text: Units of one product sold per day, zero on most days
choices.why: Yes. A truth of zero makes the division undefined.

choices.text: The price of a box in reais
choices.why: Prices are well away from zero.

choices.text: Monthly revenue of a large shop
choices.why: Large and never zero; MAPE works there.

choices.text: Delivery minutes, which on these test months are never below 15
choices.why: No truth near zero, so the division is safe.

prompt: A constant guess of 60 minutes scored R² = −0.732. What does a negative R² mean?

choices.text: A calculation error
choices.why: R² has no lower limit; negative is legitimate.

choices.text: Worse than predicting the test rows' mean
choices.why: Yes. Its squared errors exceed those of the mean.

choices.text: The model predicts the opposite of the truth
choices.why: A constant predicts nothing at all, in either direction.

choices.text: The data has more deliveries above 60 minutes than below
choices.why: Most deliveries are below 60.

prompt: The line's R² is 0.397 with the stuck deliveries and 0.870 without them. Why is that a weakness of R²?

choices.text: It shows the line is overfitted
choices.why: Nothing here compares training and test.

choices.text: R² should be computed on training rows
choices.why: Training rows would flatter the model.

choices.text: The same model gets very different scores depending on the rows asked about
choices.why: Yes. R² mixes the model's errors with the spread of the data.

choices.text: The stuck deliveries are fake
choices.why: They are real delays nobody could predict.

prompt: `boost_absolute` predicts the median. Roughly what share of its promises would you expect to be late, in percent?
The average of truth minus prediction, keeping the sign, is called the ___ of the model.
Why is the line late only 26.6% of the time when shown as a promise?
hint: Where does the mean sit here?

choices.text: It has the best MAE of the four models
choices.why: `boost_absolute` has the best MAE.

choices.text: It was designed as a cautious promise
choices.why: Nobody designed it for promises; it fits the mean.

choices.text: Linear models are biased towards early arrivals
choices.why: Its bias is almost zero.

choices.text: The mean sits above the median on this data
choices.why: Yes. The tail pulls the mean up, which happens to help.

prompt: A late minute costs three times an early minute. Which quantile should the promise model predict? Two decimal places.
Order the quantile models from `promise.py` by how often they were late, most often first.
hint: A higher quantile promises more time.

prompt: Even the 0.95 model is more than ten minutes late on 2.9% of deliveries. Why?

choices.text: They are the stuck vans, which no column predicts
choices.why: Yes. A flat tyre is not in the data.

choices.text: The test months are rainier than training
choices.why: Rain is a column the model reads.

choices.text: Quantile regression ignores the largest errors when it fits
choices.why: It weighs every late minute by 0.95.

choices.text: The quantile was set too low for this data
choices.why: Raising it further would make every promise absurd to cover a few vans.

prompt: Which of these are true of the 0.9 quantile model on the test months? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It promised about 7 minutes more than the median model
choices.why: Yes, 48.4 against 41.4.

choices.text: It has the best MAE
choices.why: Leaning late costs MAE; the median model wins that.

choices.text: It was late on 13.7% of deliveries
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: It was late on exactly 10% of deliveries
choices.why: The quantile is approximate on new months.

prompt: Which pair did Feira em Casa end up using?

choices.text: Whichever model has the highest R² each month
choices.why: R² is the RMSE in disguise and answers neither question.

choices.text: The 0.9 quantile in the app; `boost_absolute` for planning
choices.why: Yes. A promise and a typical time are different questions.

choices.text: The line for everything
choices.why: It is neither the typical time nor a promise.

choices.text: `boost_absolute` in the app, because it has the best MAE
choices.why: It is late half the time.

prompt: A colleague reports "MAE 5.0 minutes" for a delivery promise model. What should be added before anybody ships it?

choices.text: The MAPE, because managers like percentages
choices.why: MAPE also discards the sign, and it likes predicting low.

choices.text: The R², so a statistician can judge it
choices.why: R² says nothing about lateness.

choices.text: The bias and the share of deliveries that arrive late
choices.why: Yes. A median model with a fine MAE is late half the time.

choices.text: The RMSE, since it is stricter
choices.why: It is stricter about big misses, not about direction.

prompt: The logistics team wants the typical delivery time for routing. Which loss should the model be fitted with?
hint: Typical means half above, half below.

choices.text: `squared_error`, the default for every regression problem anybody will meet
choices.why: The default aims at the mean, which the tail pulls up.

choices.text: `quantile` at 0.95
choices.why: That is a cautious promise, not the typical time.

choices.text: Whichever gives the highest R²
choices.why: R² rewards the mean, like squared error.

choices.text: `absolute_error`
choices.why: Yes. It aims at the median.
